title: Know your rights at work.
intro: Short, clear information. Open a card for details and exceptions.
sectionIntro: Rules can differ by industry and collective agreement.
helpText: Keep your documents and ask for free advice. Ask questions before signing anything you do not understand.
disclaimer: This page gives general information, not legal advice. Discuss your situation with the Arbeiterkammer (AK) or a trade union.
footer: Sources: Arbeiterkammer (AK), Österreichischer Gewerkschaftsbund (ÖGB), Gewerkschaftlicher Linksblock (GLB), kollektivvertrag.at, and RIS. Rules can change; contact your workplace representative, trade union, or source for current information. RIS publishes official Austrian laws in German.

cards.title: Collective agreements
cards.teaser: Check minimum pay and working conditions.
cards.intro: Collective agreements set minimum pay and working conditions in many industries.
bullets: The applicable agreement mainly depends on the employer’s industry and your employee category. Ask your employer which one applies.
Search by industry, region, and type of employment. Your job title alone may not identify the right agreement.
Austria has no single statutory minimum wage for everyone. Check the pay table in the applicable agreement.
A 13th and 14th salary are provided in many industries by collective or employment agreements; the law does not automatically guarantee them to everyone.

cards.title: Working hours
cards.teaser: Record when you start and finish work.
cards.intro: The statutory standard is 40 hours a week and 8 hours a day. Many collective agreements set less; 38.5 hours is common.
bullets: 38.5 hours does not apply to everyone. Hours depend on the industry agreement and employee category. Some jobs also have special shift rules.
Your employer must record working time. Keep your own records too and ask for a copy.
If you work more than 6 hours a day, you generally get a break of at least 30 minutes.
There is generally an 11-hour rest period between work shifts. Some industries have exceptions and compensatory-rest rules.

cards.title: Overtime and breaks
cards.intro: Extra work should not go unpaid. Record your hours and your manager’s instructions.
bullets: Overtime generally earns at least a 50% premium or equivalent time off. A collective agreement may provide more.
There are legal limits and exceptions. The general maximum, including overtime, is 12 hours a day and 60 hours a week; the longer-term average is usually no more than 48 hours a week.
For part-time work, extra hours are not always overtime in the legal sense. Different rules may apply.
Keep your payslips, shift schedules, and time records.

cards.title: Annual leave and public holidays
cards.teaser: Check your leave and holiday pay.
cards.intro: Most employees are entitled to 5 weeks of paid annual leave.
bullets: With a five-day week, this is usually 25 working days. Under certain conditions, entitlement rises to 6 weeks after long service.
Agree on leave dates with your employer. Do not take leave without approval; unused days do not automatically disappear.
If you do not work on a public holiday, your pay usually continues. Special rules for working on a holiday depend on the law and collective agreement.
When employment ends, you may be entitled to payment for unused leave.

cards.title: Sick leave and care leave
cards.teaser: Tell your employer as soon as possible.
cards.intro: If you cannot work, notify your employer without delay.
bullets: Your employer may ask for a medical certificate from the first day. Get it in time.
Pay may continue for a period during illness. The duration depends on service and your circumstances.
Pflegefreistellung is short-term paid care leave. Pflegekarenz and Pflegeteilzeit are separate, longer care-leave or reduced-hours arrangements. Ask the AK to check the conditions for your case.
Keep messages to your employer and medical documents.

cards.title: Starting work, pay, and leaving a job
cards.teaser: Get copies of documents and keep them.
cards.intro: Confirm your pay, working hours, and duties before you start work.
bullets: Your employer must register you for social insurance before you start. Ask for a copy of the registration.
If there is no written employment contract, your employer must give you a Dienstzettel with the essential terms. Ask before signing anything you do not understand.
Check your payslips and bank payments. Ask in writing if pay is missing, and keep your records.
Notice periods and formal rules can apply to dismissal or resignation. Contact the AK or a union before a deadline.

cards.title: Work clothes and changing time
cards.teaser: Required changing time may count as working time.
cards.intro: If your employer requires specific clothing or protective equipment and you must change at work, the changing time may count as working time.
bullets: This does not apply automatically to every job. It matters whether the clothing is required and whether you must change at the workplace.
Record changing time as well as your start and finish times.
A collective agreement or workplace rules may add conditions. Ask the AK or a union about your situation.

cards.title: Children and family rights
cards.teaser: Check maternity protection, parental leave, and family benefits.
cards.intro: Having a child can bring different leave rights and family benefits.
bullets: Mutterschutz, Elternkarenz, and Elternteilzeit are different rights. Notice deadlines apply; ask the AK before sending written notice to your employer.
Kinderbetreuungsgeld and Familienbeihilfe are separate family benefits. Eligibility may depend on residence and other conditions.
Papamonat and leave for childcare have specific conditions. Check the current rules with the AK.

cards.title: Tax and payslips
cards.teaser: Check whether you may be due a tax refund.
cards.intro: Tax and social insurance contributions are deducted from your pay. Check your payslip regularly.
bullets: The Arbeitnehmerveranlagung (employee tax assessment) may allow you to reclaim some overpaid wage tax.
Tax benefits such as Familienbonus and Pendlerpauschale depend on eligibility and are not automatic for everyone.
Gross pay, net pay, tax, and social insurance contributions are different items. Ask the AK if you do not understand your payslip.
